title: MultiCare's $700 Million Pledge for Oregon's Samaritan Hospitals Comes with State Conditions Patients Can Track Over 10 Years
text:
MultiCare's $700 Million Pledge for Oregon's Samaritan Hospitals Comes with State Conditions Patients Can Track Over 10 Years
Samaritan Health Services, the five-hospital system serving Corvallis, Albany, Lebanon, Lincoln City, and Newport, will join Tacoma, Washington-based MultiCare Health System on Nov. 1. The deal comes with a $700 million, 10-year investment pledge, and Oregon's approval attaches conditions that require regular reports on whether that money is spent.
All public agencies reviewing the deal have approved it or announced their intent to, according to an Oct. 12 joint release reported by Becker's Hospital Review. Samaritan serves more than 290,000 residents in the mid-Willamette Valley and on the central coast and will keep its name, local leadership, and community-based governance. MultiCare operates 13 hospitals in Washington and more than 300 care locations across Washington, Idaho, and Oregon.
For patients, the stakes are concrete. The money is meant to pay for new urgent care centers, more specialists, and expanded hospital capacity. Large hospital pledges can shrink or shift over time, which is why the state's monitoring rules matter as much as the headline number.
The Conditions Behind the $700 Million
The Oregon Health Authority's order approving the transaction, issued Aug. 24 through its Health Care Market Oversight program, approved the deal with conditions. MultiCare must spend at least $300 million of the pledge in the first five years, regardless of Samaritan's financial performance.
The planned projects include renovating and expanding Good Samaritan Regional Medical Center in Corvallis and recruiting physicians and advanced practice providers in fields such as primary care, behavioral health, and pediatrics. The order also lists an off-campus emergency department in or near Albany, one or two ambulatory surgery centers, six to eight urgent care centers based on patient demand, four to eight outpatient rehabilitation centers, and one or two outpatient imaging centers.
For five years after closing, MultiCare must use "commercially reasonable efforts" to maintain nine hospital services without significant reduction. They include 24-hour emergency care, trauma services, intensive care, birthing services, pharmacy, imaging, and laboratory services. Samaritan must also stay enrolled in Medicare and Oregon Medicaid, keep financial assistance policies, and avoid "all-or-nothing" contracting that forces insurers to contract with every Samaritan hospital.
The order also requires the parties to honor commitments in their affiliation agreement that protect local control. MultiCare cannot sell all of Samaritan's assets substantially or dissolve Samaritan or its hospitals for seven years after closing without the Samaritan board's approval, and it must add an Oregon representative to its own board. For five years, Samaritan's profits cannot be used to fund MultiCare operations outside Oregon.
If the board decides to end or significantly reduce a protected service, the state must be notified within 15 days. The order defines a significant reduction as a change of one-third or more in standard service measures set in state rules.
There are limits. The order sets no price caps, and it says the parties may change the capital plan "at any time and for any reason." However, any proposed reduction of the $700 million or extension of the 10-year timeline must be reported to the state within 10 business days.
Paper Trail Patients Can Follow
The order builds in several public checkpoints. The parties must submit a capital commitment plan to the state, post a public summary on Samaritan's website, and give a copy to each local Samaritan hospital board. A compliance officer must be appointed within 30 days of closing.
Annual compliance reports to the state are required for 10 years. Each must certify compliance with every condition and describe capital spending and financial measures. For the first five years, the reports must also list insurer contract changes and include staffing data.
Oregon law adds a second layer. Under the state's follow-up review guidance for completed transactions, the Oregon Health Authority analyzes completed deals one, two, and five years after closing. It checks compliance with conditions and cost trends, then publishes its findings in a public report. Public comments are accepted throughout each review, and violations can bring civil penalties of up to $10,000 per offense.
With a Nov. 1 closing, the first of those reviews would fall around November 2027. Residents can sign up for updates or submit comments by email, voicemail, or online form through the Health Care Market Oversight program.
Rural Patients and a Strained System
Residents of smaller coastal and valley communities who rely on Samaritan for emergency and maternity care have the most at stake, along with Medicaid members and patients who travel long distances to see specialists. Samaritan also runs Samaritan Health Plans and the InterCommunity Health Network, a coordinated care organization that serves Medicaid members in the region.
Financial pressure drove the deal. Samaritan lost about $40 million in 2025 after losing about $68 million in 2024, according to the Lincoln Chronicle. U.S. Bank issued a default notice in June 2025 after Samaritan's reserves fell below levels it had promised bondholders. In June 2026, Samaritan asked bondholders to waive the notice, and CEO Marty Cahill said removing it "removes meaningful impediments" to closing the deal.
Samaritan has said there are no planned changes to the insurance plans it accepts through 2027, according to its announcement of the state's approval. Patients should still confirm before appointments that their doctor and plan are unchanged, especially during fall open enrollment.
Patients who notice a service closing or moving farther away can report it to the oversight program, and community members can ask local hospital boards for the capital plan once it is shared. MultiCare's capital plan and Samaritan's first annual compliance report will show whether early projects, such as the Albany emergency department and new urgent care centers, are on track.
Key Questions Answered
When does Samaritan join MultiCare? The affiliation takes effect Nov. 1, 2026, with a phased integration. Samaritan keeps its name, local leadership, and community-based governance.
What is MultiCare promising? MultiCare pledged $700 million over 10 years, with at least $300 million in the first five years. Planned projects include expanding Good Samaritan Regional Medical Center, recruiting providers, and opening new outpatient sites.
Can the investment pledge change? Yes. The plan can be modified, but any proposed reduction of the $700 million or extension of the timeline must be reported to the Oregon Health Authority within 10 business days.
How can patients track the commitments? A public summary of the capital plan must be posted on Samaritan's website, annual compliance reports are required for 10 years, and the state publishes follow-up reviews at one, two, and five years after closing.
Will my insurance still work at Samaritan? Samaritan says no changes to the insurance plans it accepts are planned through 2027. Patients should still confirm with their plan and doctor's office before appointments.
Where can residents raise concerns? Residents can contact the Oregon Health Authority's Health Care Market Oversight program by email, voicemail, or its online comment form, and can sign up for program updates.
Published by Medicaldaily.com
